name: Hamstrings
func: Three muscles on the back of the thigh. They bend the knee and pull the thigh backward at the hip, and they brake the swinging leg when you run.

levels.kid:
The **hamstrings** are the muscles on the **back of your thigh**. There are **three** of them, side by side.

They start at the bone you sit on and go down to just below your knee. When they squeeze, they **bend your knee**, like when you kick your heel up toward your bottom. They also help pull your leg **backward** when you walk and run.

If you try to touch your toes with straight legs, the stretchy feeling on the back of your legs is your hamstrings! Fast runners have to take good care of them.
levels.hs:
The **hamstrings** are the three muscles of the **back (posterior compartment)** of the thigh:

**Biceps femoris**, on the outer (lateral) side, has a **long head** and a **short head**.
**Semitendinosus**, on the inner side, has a long, cord-like tendon.
**Semimembranosus**, deep to semitendinosus on the inner side, has a flat, membrane-like upper tendon.

Except for the short head of biceps femoris, they all start on the **ischial tuberosity**, the bony bump you sit on. The short head starts on the back of the femur (the **linea aspera**).

Biceps femoris inserts on the **head of the fibula** on the outside of the knee. Semitendinosus inserts on the inner upper tibia as part of the **pes anserinus**, and semimembranosus inserts on the back of the **medial tibial condyle**. Their tendons form the sides of the diamond-shaped hollow behind the knee, the **popliteal fossa**.

Because most of them cross both the hip and knee, they **extend the hip** and **flex the knee**. They are supplied by the **sciatic nerve**: the tibial part supplies most, while the common fibular part supplies the short head of biceps femoris. The **adductor magnus** lies on their inner side and the quadriceps in front.
levels.college:
**Attachments:** semitendinosus and the long head of biceps femoris share a **conjoint tendon** from the upper inner part of the ischial tuberosity; semimembranosus arises from its upper outer facet. The short head of biceps arises from the lateral lip of the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line. Semitendinosus joins sartorius and gracilis at the **pes anserinus**; semimembranosus has several insertions, including the **oblique popliteal ligament** and an attachment to the medial meniscus, which it pulls back during flexion.

**Innervation:** the **tibial division** of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2) supplies semitendinosus, semimembranosus, the long head of biceps and the hamstring part of **adductor magnus**; the **common fibular division** supplies the short head of biceps. This split matters: in a sciatic injury, the short head may be affected differently.

**Rotation:** with the knee flexed, biceps femoris **laterally rotates** the leg, while semitendinosus and semimembranosus **medially rotate** it.

**Relations:** the sciatic nerve runs down the back of the thigh deep to the long head of biceps femoris, dividing into the tibial and common fibular nerves usually at the apex of the popliteal fossa. The **popliteal artery and vein** pass through the fossa deep to the nerves. Blood supply comes from **perforating branches of the profunda femoris** and the inferior gluteal artery.

**Function in gait:** the hamstrings are most active in **late swing**, when they contract while lengthening (eccentrically) to decelerate the forward-swinging shank and prepare for foot strike, and in early stance to extend the hip.
levels.phd:
Hamstring strain is the most common injury in sprinting sports, and research focuses on why. The leading model is **eccentric overload in late swing**: motion capture and musculoskeletal modelling show the **long head of biceps femoris** reaches its peak stretch and high force just before foot strike. Its fascicles are relatively short and arranged in a pennate pattern, and its dual innervation (tibial for the long head, fibular for the short head) has been hypothesised to cause poorly synchronised contraction, though evidence for this is debated.

Injury sites vary. Most acute strains occur at the **musculotendinous junction**, especially at the proximal long head of biceps femoris. Injuries involving the **intramuscular tendon** have longer recovery and higher re-injury rates, a key finding from MRI grading systems such as the **British Athletics Muscle Injury Classification**.

Prevention trials show that eccentric strengthening, most famously the **Nordic hamstring exercise**, substantially reduces injury rates in football players, likely by increasing fascicle length and eccentric strength. Implementation in real teams remains a challenge.

Semitendinosus regenerates remarkably after harvest. When its tendon is taken for **ACL reconstruction**, MRI studies show regeneration of a tendon-like structure in many patients within months to a year, though the muscle often retracts and loses some deep knee flexion strength.

Hamstring tightness is often measured with the straight-leg raise. Flexibility depends more on **stretch tolerance** (a sensory/nervous system change) than on actual increases in muscle length, a finding that reshaped thinking about stretching.
levels.expert:
**Exam:** inspect for bruising on the back of the thigh, palpate along the muscle for a gap, and test knee flexion strength in prone. Pain on passive straight-leg raise or with resisted flexion suggests a strain; the **Askling H-test** and slump test help distinguish muscle injury from neural tension.

**Proximal hamstring avulsion** (tendon torn from the ischial tuberosity) occurs with forceful hip flexion with the knee straight, as in water skiing or a slip into the splits. Patients report a pop and sitting pain, and bruising tracks down the thigh. **MRI** confirms the number of tendons involved and retraction. Complete avulsions with retraction are commonly repaired surgically, ideally early; the **sciatic nerve** lies close and can be scarred.

**Ischial apophysis avulsion** occurs in adolescent athletes, as the growth plate is weaker than the tendon; an X-ray shows a displaced bone fragment.

**Hamstring tendinopathy** gives deep buttock pain on sitting and running uphill.

**Sciatic nerve lesions** in the thigh weaken knee flexion and all muscles below the knee. In contrast, an **L5 radiculopathy** spares most hamstring strength, and an **S1 radiculopathy** may weaken the hamstrings slightly and reduce the ankle reflex.

**Hamstring autograft** (semitendinosus, often with gracilis) is a standard graft for ACL reconstruction.

In children with **cerebral palsy**, tight hamstrings cause a crouched gait, and surgical lengthening may be part of multilevel surgery.

The **medial hamstring reflex** (L5) and **lateral hamstring reflex** (S1) are occasionally used to localise radiculopathy.

keyPoints: Three muscles: biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus
Most start on the ischial tuberosity
Extend the hip and flex the knee
Sciatic nerve: tibial part, except the short head of biceps (common fibular)
Commonest sprint injury, in late swing; Nordic exercise reduces risk

test.q: Which bony landmark do most hamstrings start from?
test.explain: The sitting bone is the common origin, except for the short head of biceps femoris.

test.q: Which hamstring inserts on the head of the fibula? (two words)
test.explain: Biceps femoris is the lateral hamstring.

test.q: The short head of biceps femoris is supplied by which part of the sciatic nerve?
test.explain: It's the only hamstring part supplied by the common fibular division.

test.q: In which phase of sprinting are hamstrings most often strained?
test.explain: They work eccentrically to slow the swinging leg just before foot strike.

test.q: Which hamstring tendon is commonly harvested for ACL reconstruction?
test.explain: It is often taken with gracilis and can partly regenerate.
